titre: Teflon Came Out of a Gas Cylinder That Refused to Open
accroche: On April 6, 1938, a DuPont technician opens the valve of a refrigerant gas cylinder: nothing comes out, and yet it still weighs its full weight.
contenu_vulgarise:
On April 6, 1938, in a DuPont laboratory in New Jersey, the chemistry assistant Jack Rebok picks up a cylinder of refrigerant gas used the day before. He opens the valve: nothing comes out. The team unscrews it completely, turns the cylinder upside down, and a whitish powder falls onto the lab bench. They scrape the inside with a wire to recover more, but the amount still does not match the weight of the cylinder, which has stayed unchanged. They then decide to cut it open: inside, more powder, packed onto the bottom and lower sides.

## A gas that transformed on its own

The chemist Roy Plunkett was then directing research on fluorinated refrigerant gases, as part of a program that had nothing to do with coatings or cooking. The gas sealed in the cylinder, tetrafluoroethylene, had transformed all by itself: its molecules had linked up with one another to form an entirely new solid, polytetrafluoroethylene, PTFE.

Plunkett could have written the incident off as a defective cylinder and ordered another. He chose instead to analyze this unexpected powder. It resists acid, fire, extreme cold, and nothing sticks durably to its surface, not even water or grease. DuPont files a patent, issued on February 4, 1941 under number US 2,230,654, and in 1945 registers the Teflon trademark for this polymer. By 1948, the Parkersburg plant, in West Virginia, is already producing more than 910,000 kilograms a year, without anyone yet having thought of coating a frying pan with it.

## A material with no use, for sixteen years

This delay is the least told part of the story. PTFE first equips industrial parts, valve seals, electrical insulators, where its resistance to the most corrosive substances and to extreme temperatures proves valuable. It is only in 1954 that the French engineer Marc Grégoire thinks of applying this coating to kitchen utensils, and in 1956 he founds the company Tefal to sell them.

Between the chemical discovery and its best-known use by the general public, sixteen years therefore pass, and two different countries. Chance produced only the first half of the story: a technician who opens a cylinder that should not be full and who, instead of throwing it away, looks at what it really contains. The second half, finding a use for a material that serves no planned purpose, required an entirely different kind of attention, in an entirely different trade.

citation.texte: On the morning of April 6, 1938, Jack Rebok, my assistant, selected one of the TFE cylinders... nothing happened... we decided to cut open the cylinder. When we did, we found more of the powder packed onto the bottom and lower sides of the cylinder.
citation.source: “The History of Polytetrafluoroethylene: Discovery and Development,” in High Performance Polymers: Their Origin and Development (R. B. Seymour and G. S. Kirshenbaum, eds.), Elsevier, 1986, pp. 261-266

carte.punch: Teflon was born from a gas cylinder that had to be cut open to understand what it contained.
carte.idee: In 1938, a DuPont technician opens a cylinder of refrigerant gas that refuses to empty. Cutting it open, the team finds a new white powder, resistant to everything. It will be another sixteen years before anyone thinks of using it for a frying pan.

quiz.question: What really transformed the gas in the cylinder into a resistant white powder?
choix: A catalyst deliberately added by Plunkett to trigger the reaction
The molecules of tetrafluoroethylene gas linked up with one another to form a solid polymer
A reaction with oxygen from air that had accidentally entered the cylinder
An extreme cooling that froze the gas into a crystalline solid
quiz.explication: Tetrafluoroethylene polymerized inside the closed cylinder: its molecules linked into long chains to form PTFE, a solid polymer, far more resistant than the starting gas.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why did the weight of the cylinder not match the amount of powder first recovered?
choix: Because a leak had made some of the gas escape before the cylinder was opened
Because the cylinder actually contained two different gases mixed together
Because the cylinder still weighed its full weight, without the scraped powder representing all of it
Because the valve itself weighed more than expected in the initial calculation
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The weight of the cylinder had stayed unchanged, but the powder recovered by scraping did not correspond to that mass, which led the team to cut the cylinder open to look for the rest.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What was Roy Plunkett’s research actually about at the time of the discovery?
choix: Fluorinated refrigerant gases, with no link to coatings or cooking
Nonstick coatings intended for kitchen utensils
Electrical insulators for the emerging automobile industry
Solvents intended for cleaning metal parts
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Plunkett was directing research on fluorinated refrigerant gases, a program that had nothing to do with the coatings or cooking where PTFE eventually found its best-known use.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How much time passed between the discovery of PTFE and its first use for a frying pan?
choix: Only two years, the time to file the DuPont patent
Sixteen years, and the passage from an American laboratory to a French engineer
More than thirty years, the time for distrust of plastics to fade
A few months, the time to patent and then commercialize the product
quiz_supplementaire.explication: PTFE was discovered in 1938 at DuPont; it was only in 1954 that the French engineer Marc Grégoire thought of applying it to kitchen utensils, sixteen years later, before founding Tefal in 1956.
